checkpoints: The core shift is reframing the problem from "compute distance faster" to "stop computing distance across everyone".
Raw lat/lng cannot be indexed because two points a meter apart are already two different float keys, and no index can run on a sqrt computation.
That indexing gap is why any radius filter degrades into an O(N) scan over a million rows for EVERY request at scale (hundreds of thousands of requests per minute).
H3's latLngToCell hashes a coordinate into ONE deterministic cell id, so every driver inside the same hexagon collapses onto that same key.
"Find drivers near a pickup point" becomes a bucket lookup for the cell containing the pickup (and its k-ring).
"How hot is this area" becomes a group-by count on that exact cell key — O(1)/O(k²) instead of O(N).
Determinism is what actually turns the id into a real key: every node, every language independently derives the same id for the same coordinate, with no coordination or synchronization needed.
Real distance/ETA is then computed only on the handful of candidates the cell/ring returns, not on the whole fleet.
The essence is turning a 2D problem into a 1D one.
A GEO key is not a special type — GEOADD key lng lat member is just ZADD with the score set to the 52-bit geohash of the coordinate, so a driver's position actually lives in an ordinary sorted set.
Geohash interleaves the bits of longitude and latitude, so two points near each other in the real world get scores near each other, landing in adjacent score ranges.
A radius query's phase one picks the few geohash cells that cover the circle, each a contiguous score range that is cheap to read.
Phase two computes each candidate's true distance and drops those outside the radius, returning results sorted ascending by distance.
This is why the query is O(log N + M) rather than an O(N) loop computing Haversine.
That complexity is a property of the structure itself, identical whether the client is ioredis, Lettuce, StackExchange.Redis, or go-redis.
An `INCR` on a per-cell demand key with no TTL or expiry does not measure live pressure — it accumulates into a running total since the key was first created, so the number only ever goes up.

Once a cell's demand pushes the multiplier past `SURGE_CAP`, `Math.min(raw, SURGE_CAP)` keeps returning the cap for the rest of the day even after real demand has dropped back to zero, because nothing ever decrements or resets the counter.

The practical effect is that riders in a cell that was busy earlier (e.g. lunch rush) get charged the day's cumulative peak price hours later, at 3am, with no live demand at all — this is an overcharge driven by stale data, not current conditions.

Making demand decay fixes the root cause: setting a TTL on the key right after incrementing it (or writing with `SET ... NX EX` so a live key isn't reset early) causes idle cells to cool back down on their own.

A more accurate alternative to a single TTL'd counter is a real sliding window — a sorted set of request timestamps trimmed with `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` — so demand reflects only recent activity rather than a single decaying value.

`const supply = SUPPLY_BASELINE` is a second, independent defect: a hard-coded constant has no relationship to how many drivers are actually free in a given cell, and does not move when a driver goes offline, gets locked by another rider, or comes back online.

Supply should instead come from a live signal — such as a bounded geo-search over active drivers (e.g. `GEOSEARCH` on a drivers geo-index) or a maintained per-cell available-driver counter updated as drivers connect, lock, and release.

The demand-decay bug is the higher-priority issue to flag in review because it directly overcharges riders for pressure that has already passed — a trust problem — while the static supply baseline is a real but secondary accuracy improvement.

A regression test for the fix should drive a cell's quotes up until the multiplier hits the cap, stop generating demand, advance the clock past the TTL or window, and then assert that the next quote's multiplier has fallen back toward 1.0.

Running GEOSEARCH with BYRADIUS and no COUNT forces Redis to walk every geohash cell touching the full radius before any distance pruning happens, so a 50km circle hands back a candidate set far larger than anything a rider match actually needs.

Capping the radius to a business-appropriate constant and adding a COUNT parameter lets Redis stop early once it has the nearest handful of sorted candidates, shrinking both the geohash cell walk and the size of the downstream candidate list.

Awaiting `redis.exists` inside a for-loop, once per candidate, is a textbook N+1 pattern: each check is its own network round-trip, so end-to-end latency grows linearly with the candidate count even though the EXISTS lookup itself is sub-millisecond work on Redis's side.

Collapsing the per-driver EXISTS calls into a single ioredis pipeline turns many sequential round-trips into exactly one, which matters more for tail latency under load than shrinking the GEO query itself, since the N+1 loop is the dominant cost.

A periodic sweeper — a cron job or a keyspace-notification listener that runs ZREM on drivers whose heartbeat has expired — keeps the GEO key itself mostly clean over time, so the per-query online filter has progressively less stale data left to check.

Reducing round-trips does not by itself prove the optimization is safe: validating it requires asserting the returned driver set is identical before and after the change for a normal-size radius, while separately confirming the round-trip count drops and p99 latency measurably improves.

The exact radius cap and COUNT value are a business tuning decision rather than a fixed technical constant — setting them too small risks under-returning drivers in sparse areas, so the numbers need to be chosen and validated against real matching needs per market.

If the sweeper falls behind on removing expired heartbeats, stale entries can still pass the per-query EXISTS filter, letting the online/offline signal drift out of sync with the GEO key between sweeper runs.

A Redis key, no matter how many shards the cluster has, is pinned to exactly one shard by hash slot - so when every rider near a stadium maps to the same H3 cell, both the `demand:<cell>` counter and the `drivers:geo` GEO key become single hot keys that funnel thousands of operations per second onto one shard while the rest of the cluster idles.

The bottleneck here is per-key operation rate, not total data volume: the number of drivers around the stadium is modest, but the INCR and GEOSEARCH calls against those two keys arrive far faster than a single key on a single shard can absorb.

Raising the H3 resolution around detected hot spots, or sub-partitioning the demand counter into several sub-keys (for example keyed by a hash of `riderId`) and summing them back on read with `mget`, spreads the same total demand across multiple keys instead of concentrating it on one.
Sharding `drivers:geo` by region (for example `drivers:geo:<regionId>`) keeps one busy area's traffic from sharing a shard with the geo index for the entire city.

Batching near-simultaneous match requests into a single `GEOSEARCH` per tick (using `pipeline()` for the round-trips) and serving `supply` from a short-lived snapshot with a 1-2s TTL cuts the number of live reads against the hot keys instead of hitting them once per rider.

Each mitigation carries a real cost: finer or more cells mean more empty cells to skip and a wider k-ring before a driver is found, batching adds a small queueing delay before a rider sees a quote, and a snapshot cache trades read relief for a bit of staleness in the reported supply figure.

Validating the fix means replaying the stadium's traffic pattern in a single-cell load test against both the original and the modified version, comparing per-key QPS and p99 latency on that one shard, and confirming nearest-driver accuracy and surge correctness have not regressed.
The design goal is hiding H3's sharp edges behind a contract that says what it means.
Expose a small surface: cellFor(lat, lng) -> CellId, neighbors(cell, k) -> CellId[], and area(cell).
Parameters are named lat and lng so no caller ever touches raw positional argument order, the same discipline that already prevents lat/lng mix-ups on the storage side.

Fix a single resolution inside the service, configured in exactly one place, so callers can't accidentally mix a resolution-9 cell with a resolution-10 cell and break grouping — resolution is an implementation detail, not a per-call argument.
Keep the concrete binding to H3 fully internal, so the engine can change (a different H3 library, or even a different index) without any caller changing.
Geometry, the internal details of geohash/H3, and pentagon handling stay inside the boundary.
The domain only needs a stable, opaque CellId type it can use as a key, plus a way to enumerate neighbours.

Expose exactly two operations — quote(pickup) -> {cell, multiplier} and request(riderId, pickup) -> an assigned driver or an explicit {matched: false} — with every atomicity and idempotency guarantee living inside request, never in the caller's hands.
quote is read-mostly: it maps the pickup to an H3 cell, bumps demand:<cell>, and returns the cell plus the computed surge multiplier — it holds no driver and commits nothing.
request internally runs the expanding-ring GEOSEARCH — [500, 1000, 2000, 5000]m — but the caller never sees the ring mechanics, only the outcome.

Two outcomes must both be first-class: either a driver is assigned and the response carries at minimum driverId, distanceMeters, and the ring it was found in, or every ring came back empty and the response is explicitly {riderId, matched: false} — the service never hangs or throws for "no driver available" because that is a normal business outcome, not a failure.

The atomic-assignment guarantee — exactly one rider ends up with any given driver even under concurrent requests — lives inside request: for each candidate GEOSEARCH returns, request attempts SET lock:driver:<id> NX EX <ttl>, and only the request that wins that atomic write proceeds to ZREM the driver and return it as assigned.

This is exactly why the lock-then-ZREM sequence must live inside request and never leak out as separate "find" then "lock" calls — a two-step exposed contract would let a caller crash between the two calls and leave a driver either double-locked or wrongly freed.

Idempotency is a separate concern from concurrency-locking: SET NX blocks concurrent requests from different riders but not one client retrying its own request after a timeout, so the contract needs a ride-scoped idempotency key (a client-supplied requestId, or assignment:<riderId>:<rideAttempt>) that request checks before running the ring search, returning the SAME earlier result if an assignment already exists instead of matching again.

Everything else — the H3 resolution, the ring radii and their order, the demand counter's key shape, the lock's TTL, and the fact that the pool is a Redis geospatial sorted set at all — stays entirely internal and can be swapped without touching a single caller.
This is a liveness bug, not a geometry bug.
drivers:geo is a sorted set recording each driver's MOST RECENT coordinate, but a sorted set has no notion of per-member TTL, so a driver who closes the app still sits in it with a stale coordinate.
GEOSEARCH has no way to know that member has "died", so it still returns it as an ordinary candidate.
The fix is a separate heartbeat layer: every time a driver pings their location, the service also runs SET driver:heartbeat:<id> EX <ttl> (e.g. 30 seconds) to mark the driver as "fresh".
The nearby query, after GEOSEARCH returns its spatial candidate set, filters each candidate again with EXISTS driver:heartbeat:<id> and keeps only the drivers still within their heartbeat window.
This separates "indexed" (has a coordinate in drivers:geo) from "online" (still pinging) — the final response should only contain drivers satisfying both.
At production scale, filtering at query time alone is not enough because drivers:geo grows unbounded as every ghost driver permanently occupies a member that never gets removed.
A periodic sweeper is needed that ZREMs members whose heartbeat has expired out of drivers:geo, keeping the key from accumulating ghosts over time.
Root cause: driver density is not uniform across the city, so no single fixed search radius is correct everywhere.
A large fixed radius over-scans downtown, pulling in and sorting far more candidates than necessary just to find a driver that was probably one block away.
A small fixed radius wrongly reports "no cars" in the suburb, where the nearest driver might genuinely be 3km out.
The fix is an expanding-ring GEOSEARCH: start tight at 500m and only widen to 1000m, then 2000m, then 5000m if the ring comes back empty, stopping at the very first ring that has a hit.
Downtown, dense drivers mean almost every ride resolves on the first 500m ring, so the design never over-scans the way a wide fixed radius would.
In the suburb, the same logic keeps widening rings until it reaches one that actually contains a driver, instead of falsely reporting no cars available.

Trade-off: this design issues up to four GEOSEARCH calls instead of one, but each call is cheap (roughly O(log N + K)) and the loop exits at the first hit, so extra calls only happen on requests that actually need them, giving better average latency than one always-wide query.

The ring list is bounded (500, 1000, 2000, 5000m) as a hard backstop; if 5km still returns nothing, the service returns an explicit matched: false rather than widening forever or hanging the request, letting the client decide whether to wait or widen the pickup area.
The argument is about neighbour geometry, not about which shape tiles a map more elegantly.
A square grid has two kinds of neighbour: 4 edge neighbours that are close, and 4 corner neighbours that are farther by a factor of √2.
This makes a "k-cell radius" not a real circle - near and far are measured unevenly depending on direction, biasing any distance or area estimate computed via a k-ring.
That same directional unevenness also biases demand aggregation done by walking cell rings, over-weighting demand pulled from one direction and under-weighting another.
A hexagon has only one kind of neighbour - all 6 edge cells are exactly equidistant from the centre - so calling gridDisk with k approximates a real circle far better than a square grid does.
That uniform hexagon geometry keeps area/distance error small and consistent in every direction, which is exactly what matters for computing a service radius.
The same uniformity is what makes demand aggregated across neighbouring hex cells fair, instead of over-counting demand in one direction and under-counting in another.

Honest caveats: pure storage-sharding use cases that never reason about neighbour distance don't care about the shape (squares bucket fine), and every H3 resolution has exactly 12 pentagon cells - usually mid-ocean, harmless, but worth guarding against with isPentagon - where the "6 equidistant neighbours" assumption itself breaks down.
